_comment: CloudFront distribution for the PNSM frontends (Person 2's HR command
centre and Person 1's mobile web build). Owned by Person 4.
aws cloudfront create-distribution --cli-input-json file://deploy/cloudfront-distribution.json
Placeholders in ANGLE BRACKETS are filled by scripts/provision_aws.py.
WHAT IS AND IS NOT BEHIND THIS DISTRIBUTION
Behind it: the static SPA bundle in S3. Immutable, fingerprinted, read by
every visitor -- exactly what an edge cache is for.
NOT behind it: the selfie bucket. Selfies are private personal data with a
90-day retention, read a handful of times by HR and never by the public.
Caching them at 400+ edge locations would spread biometric images across
the world to save a latency nobody is waiting on, and an invalidation is
not a deletion. They stay in S3 behind short-lived presigned URLs.
See docs/DECISIONS.md D-14.
NOT behind it: the API. Every route is authenticated, uncacheable and
mutating; an edge cache in front of /v1/verify is a correctness hazard,
not an optimisation.
SHAPE: create-distribution takes {"DistributionConfig": {...}}, not the
config fields at the top level. It is the one CLI input in this directory
that is wrapped, and a flat file is rejected with a message that names a
missing parameter rather than the missing wrapper.

DistributionConfig.Comment: PNSM frontends - SPA over S3 with origin access control

_comment_oac: S3OriginConfig with an empty OriginAccessIdentity plus an
OriginAccessControlId is the modern pattern: the bucket stays fully
private with Block Public Access on, and only this distribution can
read it (SigV4-signed origin requests). The legacy alternative --
an S3 website endpoint -- requires a public bucket, which is
precisely the misconfiguration OWASP A02 is about.

_comment_policies: AWS managed policy ids, stable across accounts:
CachingOptimized forwards no cookies and no query string, which is
right for a static bundle and also means no per-user data can end up

_comment_custom_errors: THE SPA REWRITE. This is the piece most deployments get wrong.
React Router owns paths like /dashboard/geofences. No such object exists
in the bucket, so S3 answers 404 -- or 403, which is what a private
bucket behind OAC actually returns, because ListBucket is not granted and
S3 will not confirm whether the key exists. Both must be rewritten to
index.html with a 200, or every deep link and every browser refresh shows
403 is listed FIRST on purpose: with Block Public Access and an OAC-only
bucket policy, 403 is the response you will actually see. A config that
handles only 404 looks correct in review and fails in production.
ErrorCachingMinTTL is 10, not 0: a genuinely missing asset should not
hammer the origin, but a stale rewrite must not survive a deploy either.
500-class errors are deliberately NOT rewritten. Turning an origin
failure into a 200 page of HTML hides an outage from every monitor that
_comment_tls: MinimumProtocolVersion TLSv1.2_2021 is the master plan's 'TLS 1.2+',
enforced at the edge rather than assumed. The certificate comes from AWS
Certificate Manager and MUST be issued in us-east-1 -- CloudFront reads
certificates from that region only, whatever region the rest of the stack
lives in. This is the single most common CloudFront provisioning failure.
sni-only avoids the dedicated-IP charge and is supported by every browser
